findings.title: to_shouty_snake_case is not idempotent: full uppercase mapping emits combining marks that are then treated as word boundaries
findings.property: converting an already shouty-snake-case string again leaves it unchanged (f(f(x)) == f(x)); output contains only alphanumerics and '_'
findings.input: "ΐ" (U+0390 GREEK SMALL LETTER IOTA WITH DIALYTIKA AND TONOS)
findings.expected: Output is a stable SHOUTY_SNAKE_CASE string; converting it again returns the same string
findings.actual: First call gives "Ι\u{308}\u{301}" (word containing combining marks, which are not alphanumeric); second call splits at the marks and returns "Ι"
findings.evidence: lib.rs: 'Word boundaries are defined by non-alphanumeric characters' and the library is 'intended to be unicode aware, internally consistent'. The uppercase() helper uses char::to_uppercase (full mapping) per word, producing non-alphanumeric combining characters inside a word, so the output of the conversion is itself re-segmented differently. Shouty-snake output of already-shouty input is expected to be a fixed point (cf. test6 SHOUTY_SNAKE_CASE => SHOUTY_SNAKE_CASE).

review.title: Case conversion of characters with multi-char uppercase mappings emits combining marks that later split words
review.reason: The behaviour is real, but the crate never promises idempotence. Word boundaries are defined purely by `char::is_alphanumeric`, so combining marks already split words in any input, including a decomposed 'é'. The `uppercase()` helper deliberately uses the full Unicode mapping, and the same effect occurs in the lowercase path ('İ' lowercases to 'i' plus U+0307). The README's 'unicode aware, internally consistent' wording is loose, and fixing this would need a new design for combining-mark handling that the project has no precedent for.

findings.title: to_snake_case drops combining marks (they are treated as word separators), so output is not a fixed point
findings.property: snake-casing an already snake-cased string leaves it unchanged (idempotence)
findings.actual: first pass gives "i\u{307}" (standard lowercase of İ), second pass gives "i" because the combining dot U+0307 is not char::is_alphanumeric and is treated as a word separator and discarded
findings.evidence: transform() splits words on !c.is_alphanumeric(); combining marks (category Mn) are not alphanumeric, so they are silently deleted or split words (e.g. NFD "cafe\u{301}" loses its accent). lowercase() itself emits such a mark for İ, so the library produces output that its own algorithm then treats as a separator. Snake case of an already-snake string is expected to be stable, as for all ASCII inputs (which passed).

review.title: to_snake_case drops combining marks (e.g. U+0307) because they are not char::is_alphanumeric
review.reason: Heck documents no idempotence guarantee. Splitting words on !char::is_alphanumeric is a deliberate design choice: the CHANGELOG says the library uses char::is_alphanumeric for word boundaries in all cases. The lowercase() output for İ and the splitter disagree, but that only shows up on a rare input. A maintainer would more likely treat dropped Mn marks, such as NFD accents, as a known Unicode limitation than as a defect in a stated contract. The repro is correct, though, and a fix that keeps Mn characters inside words would be small and harmless, so this is a low-severity wart rather than a clear rejection.
